title: If Not STen Scores Alone, Then What? What Teachers Should Be Looking For
author: ReadWriteJen
summary: Writing as both a teacher and the parent of a daughter diagnosed with dyslexia at sixteen, ReadWriteJen argues that strong standardised reading scores (STen 8s and 9s in her daughter's case) can mask significant underlying literacy difficulty, and lays out what classroom teachers should track alongside test data. Her framework centers on five component skills — letter-sound knowledge, phonemic awareness, decoding, spelling, and oral reading fluency — each with concrete, observable warning signs a teacher can notice without formal diagnostic training, such as a child who recognises a letter-sound correspondence in a phonics lesson but cannot retrieve it later, or who spells a word correctly on a Friday test but misspells it the following week in independent writing. She singles out spelling as the single richest source of evidence because, unlike reading, it gives no visual scaffold and forces a child to draw on stored phonemic, orthographic, and morphological knowledge. The piece is emphatic that a single hesitation or slip means little; what matters is a persistent pattern across time and a child's response to high-quality explicit teaching, and that a formal diagnostic threshold should never be a precondition for starting targeted support. She closes by noting that early identification is structurally easier in primary school, where one teacher sees a child across the whole day, than in post-primary, where the picture is scattered across subject teachers who may each notice only a fragment unless they compare notes.
points: Central claim: standardised scores like STen are not inaccurate but incomplete — they reassured the author's family for years while masking a literacy difficulty later diagnosed as dyslexia, so schools should triangulate test scores with classroom evidence rather than relying on either alone.

She names five component skills teachers can directly observe for early warning signs — letter-sound knowledge, phonemic awareness, decoding, spelling, and oral reading fluency — each with specific behavioural markers rather than vague 'struggles with reading' language.

Spelling is flagged as the most diagnostically valuable evidence source because it has no visual scaffold, and she distinguishes genuine spelling knowledge from short-term test recall, citing a child who spells a word correctly on Friday's test but misspells it the next week in independent writing.

The article insists persistence over time matters more than any single data point, and explicitly argues a child should never have to meet a formal diagnostic threshold before receiving targeted intervention.

She identifies a structural post-primary blind spot: because different subject teachers each see only a fragment of a student's literacy profile (weak spelling in geography, slow reading in science, an oral/written gap in English), the pattern is invisible unless teachers actively compare observations.
quotes: My daughter's STen scores were not inaccurate. She performed well relative to her peers on the skills assessed on that particular assessment. The issue was allowing those scores to reassure us that there was no significant underlying literacy difficulty.
Although a single hesitation on its own tells us very little; it's the persistence of a pattern that tells us far more.

A child experiencing difficulties may be able to memorise ten words for Friday and reproduce them accurately, but then continue to spell these same words incorrectly in their independent writing the following week.
The most important message here is that a child does not need to meet a diagnostic threshold before receiving targeted intervention.

John's geography teacher might notice his weak spelling, his science teacher his slow reading, and his English teacher the marked difference between his oral contributions in class and his written work. Each teacher has noticed something important, but unless these observations are shared, no one may see the pattern as a whole.
Spelling can tell us an enormous amount about what a child understands because, unlike reading, the word is not already there on the page for them.
That is the limitation of using any single score as the basis for decisions about providing children with additional support.
